content: Using ai, I think I formalized stochastic calculus in Lean 4 (4600+ lines, zero sorry, one axiom) using an operator-adjoint approach: define D := δ* and derive Clark-Ocone, Itô formula, Malliavin derivative, Stein's lemma, and more from Hilbert space theory. Covers fBM for all H ∈ (0,1). Companion to a paper. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18624822. Happy to receive feedback please and thank you
You can find the lean in the Zenodo link. I'm new to this so feedback, again, appreciated.

Just commenting on the Stein's lemma and Gaussian Integration by Parts and the related axiom, you may be interested in the existing and more principled/general implementation here (leveraging the formalization of Fernique and Cameron-Martin theorem by Remy Degenne eg #26291 ).
Also the Brownian Motion project represents how some of these results should fit in mathlib
Thank you Matteo. I'll check out #26291 and the BM project. I wasn't sure what was available so totally open to refactoring.

No doubt ai did the heavy lifting here. However my dissertation instantiated this idea. Start with Clark-Ocone go to Ito over 20 year ago by hand. https://etd.ohiolink.edu/acprod/odb_etd/ws/send_file/send?accession=kent1271438954&disposition=inline. Start on page 14. Chain rule is a trap though. Forces you into Gaussian world.
Good god... 26 years ago.
16 haha
Folks, I made another round of updates on the lean. It was missing pointwise Ito formula amongst other things.

Folks, I extended to Banach spaces and Levy Processes. The lean can be found here: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18625711 (BanachLevyComplete.lean) along with the paper. Once again feedback very much appreciated!

When sharing Lean code, it is typically crucial to share it as a repository, extra helpful if it has an annotated blueprint.

Otherwise it is very hard to give feedback, note that at the moment if you put your one-file code into https://live.lean-lang.org/ , it doesn't compile.
